t: The perineum, external genitalia and lymph drainage
sub: Below the pelvic floor, one membrane splits two pouches, one nerve serves the whole region, and lymph follows embryology rather than distance.

pretest.q: After a straddle injury tears the spongy urethra, leaking urine swells the scrotum but spares which region?
pretest.why: Colles fascia fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament and with the back edge of the perineal membrane, so urine in the superficial pouch is channeled into the scrotum, penis and abdominal wall but cannot enter the thighs.

w.Penis: Colles fascia continues as the dartos layer of the penis, so the penile shaft swells with urine after this injury.
w.Lower abdominal wall: Colles fascia is continuous with Scarpa fascia of the abdominal wall, so urine climbs freely onto the lower abdomen.
w.Perineum: The superficial pouch lies in the urogenital triangle of the perineum itself, so perineal swelling is expected rather than spared.

pretest.q: Which nerve block, placed beside the ischial spine, numbs most of the perineum for delivery?
pretest.why: The pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) hooks around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament before entering the pudendal canal, so anesthetic placed beside the spine, felt through the vaginal wall, blocks most perineal sensation.

w.Ilioinguinal nerve block: The ilioinguinal nerve supplies only the mons and anterior labia, so it is added when the front of the vulva must also be numbed.
w.Obturator nerve block: The obturator nerve runs along the side wall to the medial thigh and supplies adductor muscles and thigh skin, not the perineum.
w.Genitofemoral nerve block: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies a small anterior area near the mons and does not reach the posterior perineum.

body: How is the perineum divided, and what fills each part?

The perineum is the diamond-shaped region below the pelvic diaphragm, bounded by the pubic symphysis in front, the ischiopubic rami and **ischial tuberosities** at the sides, and the sacrotuberous ligaments and the coccyx behind. A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into two triangles. The **urogenital triangle** in front lies in a horizontal plane and holds the urethra and external genitalia. The **anal triangle** behind lies in a nearly vertical plane and holds the anal canal, the external anal sphincter and the fat-filled ischioanal fossae, which let the canal expand during defecation and the perineum stretch at birth.

Across the urogenital triangle stretches the {{rp2_permem|perineal membrane}}, a tough sheet attached to the ischiopubic rami at the sides, to the pubic arch in front, where it thickens into the transverse perineal ligament, and to the perineal body behind; the urethra, and in women the vagina, pierce it. The **deep perineal pouch** above it holds the external urethral sphincter, the deep transverse perineal muscle, the membranous urethra and bulbourethral glands in men, and the dorsal nerves and vessels of the penis or clitoris. The **superficial perineal pouch** below it holds the roots of the erectile bodies, the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles, the superficial transverse perineal muscles and, in women, the Bartholin glands. It is closed below by {{rp2_colles|Colles fascia}}.
External urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscle, membranous urethra, bulbourethral glands
Bulb and crura, spongy urethra, three muscles
Vestibular bulbs, clitoral crura, Bartholin glands, three muscles
Fat, pudendal canal, inferior rectal nerve and vessels
Why does a straddle injury spread urine into the scrotum but not the thighs?

Colles fascia is the membranous layer of superficial fascia in the perineum. It attaches to the ischiopubic rami and the back edge of the perineal membrane, and in front it continues as the dartos of the penis and scrotum and as Scarpa fascia on the abdominal wall, which fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament. When a fall astride a beam tears the spongy urethra below the membrane, urine extravasates into the superficial pouch and follows that sleeve into the scrotum, penis and lower abdominal wall, but never into the thighs or the anal triangle. This **urethral rupture** pattern is the classic test of the fascial planes.
A pelvic fracture does not fill the scrotum

A pelvic fracture shears the **membranous urethra** above the perineal membrane, so urine leaks into the deep pouch and up into the **retropubic** space around the bladder, and the scrotum often stays dry. Blood at the meatus or a high-riding prostate calls for a retrograde urethrogram before anyone passes a catheter.
What are the parts of the external genitalia?

The vulva starts at the mons pubis, a fat pad over the pubic symphysis. The hair-bearing **labia majora**, where the round ligaments end, enclose the thinner **labia minora**, and the space between the labia minora is the **vestibule**. Into it open the external urethral orifice in front and the vaginal orifice behind it, partly rimmed by the hymen, a thin mucosal fold. An imperforate hymen blocks menstrual flow and causes primary amenorrhea with cyclic pelvic pain and a bulging bluish membrane.

The ducts of the Bartholin (greater vestibular) glands open at about 4 and 8 o'clock, posterolateral to the vaginal orifice. The glands lie in the superficial pouch and secrete mucus for lubrication during arousal; a blocked duct forms a cyst or abscess. The vestibular bulbs, erectile tissue along the sides of the vaginal opening, swell with arousal. The clitoris has a glans, a body of paired corpora cavernosa and two crura.

The penis has a root and a body. The root, in the superficial pouch, is the bulb of the penis in the midline and a crus on each ischiopubic ramus. The crura continue as the two **corpora cavernosa**, which fill with blood in erection, and the bulb continues as the **corpus spongiosum**, which carries the urethra and expands into the glans. Each erectile body is wrapped in a dense tunica albuginea, and a fold of skin, the prepuce, covers the glans. The male urethra has three parts: the prostatic urethra; the short **membranous urethra** in the deep pouch and external urethral sphincter; and the long spongy urethra, which widens in the bulb and again in the glans as the navicular fossa. Apart from the external meatus, the membranous part is the narrowest and least stretchy, so catheters and pelvic fractures injure it.
How do the pudendal nerve and vessels reach the perineum?

The **pudendal nerve** (S2 to S4) and the internal pudendal artery leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis, hook around the **ischial spine** and sacrospinous ligament, and re-enter through the lesser sciatic foramen. They then run forward in the {{rp2_alcock|pudendal canal}} (Alcock canal), a split in the obturator fascia on the side wall of the ischioanal fossa. The nerve gives the inferior rectal nerve to the external anal sphincter and perianal skin; the perineal nerve, whose deep branch supplies the perineal muscles and external urethral sphincter and whose superficial branch gives posterior labial or posterior scrotal nerves to the skin; and the dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris. The palpable spine guides a **pudendal block** in labor.

A pudendal block leaves the front of the perineum sensitive, because the mons and anterior labia or scrotum are supplied by the **ilioinguinal** nerve (L1). The internal pudendal artery gives inferior rectal, perineal, bulb and dorsal branches and the deep artery of the penis or clitoris, whose helicine arteries open into the erectile sinusoids and fill them in erection. The external pudendal arteries from the femoral artery supply the anterior scrotum and labia, and the deep dorsal vein of the penis drains under the pubic symphysis into the prostatic venous plexus.

The bladder outlet has two sphincters. The **internal urethral sphincter** at the bladder neck is smooth muscle: sympathetic fibers from the hypogastric nerves close it through alpha-1 receptors, which keeps semen out of the bladder, and alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin relax it. The **external urethral sphincter** is skeletal muscle under voluntary pudendal control.

The anal canal repeats the pattern. The **internal anal sphincter** is thickened smooth muscle that keeps the canal closed without effort; the **external anal sphincter** is skeletal muscle supplied by the inferior rectal nerve and squeezed on purpose. Both anchor to the {{rp2_perbody|perineal body}}, the fibromuscular knot between the anal canal and the vagina or bulb where the perineal muscles meet. Childbirth can tear it: a second-degree laceration reaches the perineal muscles, a third-degree tear the anal sphincter, and a fourth-degree tear the rectal mucosa. A mediolateral episiotomy cuts away from the midline to spare the perineal body and sphincter.
How do the autonomic nerves run erection and emission?

Autonomic fibers reach the pelvic and perineal organs through the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Sympathetic fibers arrive through the lumbar splanchnic nerves and cause vasoconstriction, closure of the internal urethral and anal sphincters and, in men, emission. Parasympathetic fibers arrive as the pelvic splanchnic nerves and cause vasodilation, contraction of the detrusor and engorgement of erectile tissue. Male sexual function strings the three kinds of nerve in sequence.
Point, squeeze, shoot: the nerves of male sexual function
**Pelvic splanchnic** nerves (S2 to S4) release nitric oxide, which relaxes penile arteries and sinusoids so the corpora fill and compress their veins against the tunica albuginea.
Hypogastric fibers from L1 and L2 contract the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate to move semen into the urethra, and close the internal urethral sphincter.
The pudendal nerve drives rhythmic contraction of the bulbospongiosus, which expels semen; damage to sympathetic fibers lets the sphincter open, causing retrograde ejaculation into the bladder.
Why does the pectinate line split the anal canal in two?

The {{rp2_pectinate|pectinate line}} marks where the endoderm of the hindgut met the ectoderm of the anal pit, so everything above and below it differs. Above the line the lining is columnar, cancers are adenocarcinomas, the superior rectal artery from the inferior mesenteric artery supplies it, its veins drain to the portal system, lymph goes to internal iliac nodes and the nerves are visceral, sensing only stretch. **Internal hemorrhoids** arise here, so they bleed but do not hurt. Below the line the lining is stratified squamous, cancers are squamous cell carcinomas, the inferior rectal vessels join the caval system, lymph goes to **superficial inguinal** nodes, and the somatic inferior rectal nerve makes **external hemorrhoids** painful.

Rectal veins join both venous systems, so the anorectal junction is a {{rp2_portocaval|portocaval anastomosis}}. In portal hypertension, blood from the superior rectal veins flows through the middle and inferior rectal veins into the caval system and swells rectal varices, which bleed but are not hemorrhoids.
Pain marks the somatic side of the line

Anything below the pectinate line, such as a thrombosed external hemorrhoid, an anal fissure or a squamous tumor, hurts because the **inferior rectal** branch of the pudendal nerve carries somatic pain. Above the line, an internal hemorrhoid or adenocarcinoma presents with painless bleeding because visceral afferents respond only to stretch.
Where does lymph from each pelvic organ drain?

Lymph runs back along the arteries that supply an organ, so distance is a poor guide. The ovaries and testes developed near the kidneys and kept their aortic vessels, so they drain to **para-aortic** nodes, and testicular cancer spreads there rather than to the groin. The uterine body, cervix and upper vagina drain with the uterine and vaginal vessels to internal iliac, external iliac and obturator nodes, and the prostate drains mainly to **internal iliac** nodes. The lower vagina, vulva, scrotum, penile shaft skin and anal canal below the pectinate line drain to the superficial inguinal nodes. The glans drains to **deep inguinal** nodes, and some fundal lymph follows the round ligament to the groin.
Cervical cancer in pelvic side-wall nodes
Scrotal abscess with tender groin nodes
Anal canal below the pectinate line

These routes explain clinical patterns. Vulvar and penile cancers spread first to the superficial inguinal nodes, so the surgeon removes the {{rp2_sentinel|sentinel node}}, the first node on the route, and examines it before deciding on a full groin dissection. Infections of the same skin enlarge the same nodes: chancroid and lymphogranuloma venereum produce tender, matted nodes that can suppurate as an **inguinal bubo**, while the chancre of primary syphilis leaves painless, rubbery nodes. Deep pelvic infections drain to iliac nodes that cannot be felt, so they give no groin signal.

body.q: After falling astride a beam, a man has swelling of the scrotum, penis and lower abdominal wall but not the thighs. Which reasoning best explains the pattern?
o: The membranous urethra tore above the perineal membrane, so urine rose through the deep pouch into the retropubic space
The bladder ruptured into the peritoneal cavity, and urine tracked down the inguinal canals into the scrotum
Urine spread through loose subcutaneous fat, which is continuous everywhere, so sparing of the thighs is chance
The spongy urethra tore below the membrane, and Colles fascia, tied to the rami and perineal membrane and continuous with Scarpa fascia, channels urine forward and upward
body.why: A straddle injury crushes the spongy urethra against the pubic arch below the perineal membrane, so urine enters the superficial pouch, whose floor is Colles fascia. That fascia is attached to the ischiopubic rami and the back of the membrane but continues into dartos and Scarpa fascia, which fuses with the fascia lata, so urine can only go forward and up. A membranous tear fills the retropubic space instead, and bladder rupture causes ascites.

body: Why does testicular cancer spread to nodes beside the aorta instead of the groin?

The testis forms on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidney and descends through the inguinal canal late in fetal life, dragging its artery, veins and lymphatics behind it. Its lymph vessels therefore climb back up the spermatic cord to the para-aortic nodes near the origin of the testicular artery. The scrotal skin is different: it is body wall that never moved, so it drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Enlarged groin nodes in testicular cancer suggest spread to the scrotal skin, one reason testes are removed through the groin rather than the scrotum.
